coherence.reasons: Both run the same sound hierarchy: allocation effect, exit cost, weak customer case, then redesign and a gated sunset. Y is tight, with four sections that each map to one executive-summary line. Its lapses are small: the summary headlines the no-migration figures ($5.5M / $3.4M) while the governing thought gives a range, and the sunset rule on slide 16 ("D acceptance + pilot shortfall = low-cost exit") sits awkwardly with its own slide 8, which shows even full migration loses $0.4M a year. X's summary lines map to page ranges, and each slide title is carried by the numbers beneath it, through to the six board decisions and two gates. X's own lapses: slide 3 says the hypothesis "survived four of five tests" when one verdict is "Unproven", and it frames "keep C" as the starting hypothesis, which reads as conclusion-first. On balance X's hierarchy is slightly more complete and internally consistent, especially the link from analysis to gate criteria.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the key's preferred recommendation (R1): retain C, redesign, fix bundle service, revisit a sunset when contracts expire. X weighs the alternatives more rigorously. It compares four options on time-phased 2027–29 cash and against each board constraint, and adds a downside redesign case (half the savings, three months late, full $0.9M spent, still +$0.40M). Gate 1 has a quantified threshold (≥$0.4M a year, tied to break-even). Gate 2 requires a validated adapter, D capacity, sustained fill, a causal renewal test and a positive exit bridge. X also answers the "redeploy to D" half of the question directly (sequence: C redesign, then D) and notes that D's spare capacity is available whether or not C exits. Y's option table is sound but thinner: annual figures only, no downside case, and a looser sunset trigger that ignores D capacity and the contribution gap. Y does handle the engineering opportunity cost more cleanly, by declining to quantify it and assigning someone to list the deferred D projects. X's illustrative $0.25M ceiling is labelled as a bound but comes close to the precision the pack warns against.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $3.8M contribution, −$2.65M recurring, −$4.75M first year, and redesign payback (X: 5.3 months and time-phased +$2.37M; Y: 44% threshold and 5.3 months). I checked X's additional arithmetic and found it correct: calendar-2027 exit of −$3.43M, −$8.7M cumulative, break-even savings of 19% and 31%, the 70% price-pressure threshold, the migration sensitivity, and the reallocated margins. X also labels its assumptions explicitly, including that the penalty counts against the $0.9M envelope and that stranded cost is split pro rata. Y states the envelope breach without flagging that assumption. Y adds one good insight (C carries 51% of shared cost on 18% of sales) and makes fewer claims overall, with only minor overreach ("bundle fill stays at 91%" under retain; reading the renewal gap as a "coverage signal"). X's overreach is stating that the bundle shortfall is "caused by A and B" as fact, which goes somewhat beyond the pack, and the illustrative engineering bound. X uses the critical evidence more fully: D capacity ceiling, penalty treated as one-time, a constraint-by-constraint test, and the bundle-fill definition. It does so without numerical errors.

revision.reasons: Both reject the CEO's immediate-exit hypothesis on the right grounds: allocated versus avoidable cost, penalties, the D capacity ceiling, and a confounded renewal correlation. Both keep the legitimate residue: a real bundle-service problem, a C effect on renewals that is neither proven nor ruled out, and a 2029 sunset left open. X goes further in showing what would have to be true for the CEO to be right: no migration rate makes exit pay, C contribution would have to fall about 70%, and Gate 2 includes a causal renewal test. It also grants the valid part of the CEO's intent by sequencing the team onto D from July. X's hypothesis table shows explicit updating ("keep C unchanged" fails and is refined to redesign). The weakness is that it frames the team's own "keep C" as the starting hypothesis rather than naming the CEO's, though it rejects the CEO's proposal explicitly elsewhere. Y addresses the CEO's claims directly and fairly, but with less depth on the conditions under which they would hold.

overall.reasons: Both documents are defensible, numerically correct and reach the key's preferred conclusion. Y is concise and clean, and would serve a board adequately. X delivers more fully what the board asked for: the margin-to-avoidable-cost walk, a quantified exit bridge with migration sensitivity, a time-phased comparison of exit, retain, delayed sunset and redesign against each constraint, a downside redesign case, a contract plan covering all nine bundle customers, explicit tests of the correlation and dashboard claims, and quantified gates. It also lists its assumptions transparently. Its extra length carries real analytical content rather than padding, and its few overstatements (A/B as the cause of the fill gap, the illustrative engineering bound, "four of five") are minor and mostly flagged.
